Avila_Marin_2011_Volumetric_Solar_Receiv.title: Volumetric receivers in Solar Thermal Power Plants with Central Receiver System technology: A review
Avila_Marin_2011_Volumetric_Solar_Receiv.system: Volumetric solar receivers (porous metallic and ceramic absorbers, open- and closed-loop configurations) used in Central Receiver System solar thermal power plants for heating air as the heat transfer fluid.
Avila_Marin_2011_Volumetric_Solar_Receiv.method: Chronological literature review compiling configurations, materials, test results, advantages and problems of numerous international/national volumetric receiver prototypes and projects.
findings: Metal absorbers achieve outlet air temperatures between 800°C and 1000°C, SiSiC ceramics up to 1200°C (silicon melts ~1400°C), and SiC up to 1500°C (limited to about 1700°C).
Receiver thermal efficiency may exceed 75% due to the volumetric effect reducing thermal radiation losses; with storage, CRS plants can operate over 4500 h/year at nominal power.
Mk-I prototype (62 mm outer diameter) delivered 3 kWth at average flux density of 1 MW/m2, producing air up to 842°C with estimated thermal efficiencies of 70–90%.

Sulzer 1 (875 mm inner diameter, 200 kWth design) achieved 780°C outlet air temperature and 200 kWth output but measured efficiency of only 68% versus a predicted 80% (Hotair code) at 550°C, due to distortion of the wire-mesh absorber causing uneven cooling.

Flow instability in highly porous honeycomb absorbers occurs above a critical solar flux given by I0,crit = 1694·β·σ·T0^4, whereas wire mesh and low-porosity ceramic foam honeycombs are stable due to quadratic-dominated pressure-loss behavior.
Avila_Marin_2011_Volumetric_Solar_Receiv.validation_data: Measured receiver outlet air temperatures, thermal efficiencies, pressure drop vs. velocity/flux behavior, and maximum material temperatures from field tests (e.g., at Plataforma Solar de Almería) tabulated for numerous prototypes (Table 2), used to compare against predicted performance (e.g., Hotair code prediction vs. measured efficiency for Sulzer 1).
Avila_Marin_2011_Volumetric_Solar_Receiv.limitations_stated: The prediction of outlet air temperatures over 1000°C for a variety of absorbers has not been completely fulfilled; unstable gas flow through volumetric receivers can lead to local overheating, poor performance and local failures such as melting or cracking; geometric distortion of some absorbers (e.g., Sulzer 1) caused insufficient cooling of some areas and lower-than-expected efficiencies; the technology has not yet been commercially developed.
Avila_Marin_2011_Volumetric_Solar_Receiv.relevance: The paper's compiled quantitative performance data (outlet temperatures, efficiencies, flux levels, pressure-drop/flow-stability behavior) and its explicit discussion of SiC's achievable temperature range (up to 1500°C, limited to ~1700°C) and honeycomb flow-instability criteria provide benchmark context and known failure modes relevant to interpreting experimental characterization of an installed SiC honeycomb receiver.

Avila_Marin_2019_review_modelling_strate.title: Modelling strategies for porous structures as solar receivers in central receiver systems: A review
Avila_Marin_2019_review_modelling_strate.system: Porous volumetric absorbers (metallic and ceramic, e.g. SiC honeycombs/foams) used as air-heated solar receivers in central receiver systems.
Avila_Marin_2019_review_modelling_strate.method: Literature review comparing detail simulation (DS) and homogeneous equivalent method (HEM) modelling strategies, including CFD and 1D models, local thermal equilibrium/non-equilibrium treatment, and radiative heat transfer calculation methods.
findings: The TSA metallic wire-mesh absorber achieved 85% thermal efficiency at an air outlet temperature of 700 °C, a concentrated solar flux of 300 kW/m2, and a recirculation ratio of 60%.

The SOLAIR ceramic (recrystallized SiC, porosity 49.5%) absorber achieved thermal efficiency of 70–75% at an air outlet temperature of 750 °C with incident solar flux in the 370–520 kW/m2 range and an air return ratio of 50%.
Livshits et al. proposed a metallic wire mesh VA candidate to reach efficiencies higher than 90%.

The review identifies HEM combined with CFD and local thermal non-equilibrium (LTNE), together with silicon carbide material and foam geometry, as the most widely used modelling strategies in the field.
Avila_Marin_2019_review_modelling_strate.ltne: Discussed as a key modelling consideration (LTE vs LTNE) in porous absorber simulation; the review states LTNE is one of the most widely used strategies in the field but does not itself report a specific magnitude or correlation.
Avila_Marin_2019_review_modelling_strate.limitations_stated: Despite numerous efforts, the theoretical volumetric effect has not been validated by experimentation; most tested volumetric absorbers presented poorer performance than predicted; it remains unclear whether ceramics are the best material choice in terms of absorber efficiency.
Avila_Marin_2019_review_modelling_strate.relevance: As a review of modelling strategies (DS vs HEM, CFD vs 1D, LTE/LTNE, radiative transfer methods) for SiC honeycomb/foam volumetric absorbers, it provides the conceptual and correlation framework (and references to specific SiC receiver studies, e.g. SOLAIR, Zaversky et al.) against which experimental characterization of an installed SiC honeycomb receiver can be interpreted and compared.

Avila_Marin_Caliot_et_al_2019_Homogeneou.title: Homogeneous equivalent model coupled with P1-approximation for dense wire meshes volumetric air receivers
Avila_Marin_Caliot_et_al_2019_Homogeneou.system: A 3D homogeneous equivalent model of open volumetric air receivers made of staggered stacks of dense metallic (alloy-310) plain-weave wire mesh screens, compared against literature experimental data.
Avila_Marin_Caliot_et_al_2019_Homogeneou.method: Volume-averaged mass, momentum (Brinkman-Forchheimer-extended Darcy) and two-temperature (LTNE) energy equations are solved with radiative transfer modeled via the P1-approximation, using coefficients (permeabilities, HTC correlations, effective conductivities, radiative properties) derived from prior experimental/numerical work, and validated against literature data for wire mesh absorbers under inhomogeneous concentrated solar flux.
findings: Six commercial AISI 310 square plain-weave wire mesh types (A-F) were characterized with wire diameters from 0.13 to 1.00 mm and mesh sizes M^-1 from 0.20 to 3.03 mm^-1, using 5 to 10 stacked screens depending on type to form single-porosity absorbers.
Maximum Reynolds number (based on hydraulic diameter and superficial velocity) was lower than 200, justifying a laminar flow assumption.
Parametric study used a uniform, parallel incident flux of 600 kW/m2, while experiment-model comparison used a measured representative solar-simulator flux profile.
Inlet fluid static temperature fixed at 300 K and reference outlet static pressure at 101325 Pa in the boundary conditions.
Effective conductivities of fluid and solid phases were modeled as keff,f = phi*kf and keff,s = (1/3)(1-phi)*ks following Schuetz & Glicksman.
Avila_Marin_Caliot_et_al_2019_Homogeneou.nu_correlation: HTC correlated as Nu_lv = a*Re^b*Pr^c (Eq. 15) using mesh hydraulic diameter as characteristic length, with coefficients a, b, c given in Table 4 for six stagger-arranged wire mesh types (numerical values not reproduced in the extracted text); correlations originate from Avila-Marin et al. [22,23] numerical work.
Avila_Marin_Caliot_et_al_2019_Homogeneou.ltne: LTNE is assumed/modeled: separate fluid and solid energy equations are solved and coupled via a volumetric convective heat transfer coefficient (hv) to account for the large temperature gradient between solid matrix and inlet air; no explicit magnitude of the fluid-solid temperature difference is stated in this excerpt.
Avila_Marin_Caliot_et_al_2019_Homogeneou.validation_data: Model results are compared against prior experimental data from Avila-Marin's own experiments/thesis [24-26], including pressure drop vs. air velocity measurements (Fig. 3, apparatus in Fig. 2) for permeability coefficients K1 and K2, and measured solar-simulator flux profiles used for the experiment-model comparison.
Avila_Marin_Caliot_et_al_2019_Homogeneou.limitations_stated: The optically thick (P1) approximation assumes the photon mean free path is short compared to mean beam length and radiation intensity tends to be isotropic, which 'could fail at the boundary'; the incident radiative flux in the experiment was actually not parallel/collimated as assumed in the model, though agreement with experiment was still good.
Avila_Marin_Caliot_et_al_2019_Homogeneou.relevance: The paper's homogeneous-equivalent/LTNE/P1 modeling framework, HTC correlations, and geometrical/optical property formulations for stacked wire-mesh absorbers provide a methodological analog and potential benchmarking approach for interpreting temperature and heat-transfer measurements from an experimentally characterized installed SiC honeycomb receiver, despite the differing absorber material and geometry (wire mesh vs. honeycomb monolith).

Avila_Marin_De_Lara_Fernandez_Reche_2018.title: Experimental results of gradual porosity volumetric air receivers with wire meshes
Avila_Marin_De_Lara_Fernandez_Reche_2018.system: Metallic (310-alloy) plain-weave wire mesh volumetric absorbers with gradual (single/double/triple) porosity, tested against reference TSA (metallic) and SOLAIR (ceramic) absorber pieces in a lab-scale solar receiver setup.
Avila_Marin_De_Lara_Fernandez_Reche_2018.method: A new 1 kWt lab-scale test bed coupled to a 4 kWe xenon short-arc solar simulator was used to test 26 optimized-thickness wire-mesh absorbers (6 single-, 12 double-, 8 triple-porosity configurations) built from six commercial 310-alloy screens plus TSA and SOLAIR reference pieces.
findings: TSA absorber (Inconel 601 knit-wire) achieved 85% design efficiency at 700°C air outlet temperature, 300 kW/m2 average flux density, and 60% air return ratio.
SOLAIR absorber (RSiC, 270 SiSiC ceramic cups, open porosity 49.5%) achieved 70-75% efficiency at 750°C outlet temperature, 370-520 kW/m2 mean flux, and 50% air return ratio.

26 gradual-porosity wire-mesh absorbers were built and tested (6 single-porosity, 12 double-porosity, 8 triple-porosity) with optimized thickness to minimize material use while achieving complete absorption.
The Catrec 2 prototype module was destroyed while attempting to exceed its achieved 460°C average air outlet temperature.
The gradual porosity wire-mesh concept shows potential to match or improve on the performance of the TSA and SOLAIR baseline absorbers.
Avila_Marin_De_Lara_Fernandez_Reche_2018.ltne: not considered in this experimental study; the authors cite a separate numerical/LTNE comparison paper (ref. [46]) but this work itself reports only experimental absorber performance without an LTNE treatment or measured non-equilibrium magnitude.
Avila_Marin_De_Lara_Fernandez_Reche_2018.validation_data: Performance data from the baseline TSA and SOLAIR absorbers (efficiency, air outlet temperature, incident flux density, air return ratio) are used as reference/benchmark values against which the new gradual-porosity wire-mesh absorbers' performance is compared.
Avila_Marin_De_Lara_Fernandez_Reche_2018.limitations_stated: The paper notes that most volumetric receivers tested in past decades (e.g., Sulzer 1, Sulzer 2, Catrec 1, Catrec 2) did not match predicted nominal conditions, operating at lower-than-expected efficiencies, and that unresolved issues remain in achieving the volumetric effect, selecting adequate porosity/geometry to avoid surface-only absorption, and optimizing absorber thickness and material durability under high solar flux.
Avila_Marin_De_Lara_Fernandez_Reche_2018.relevance: The paper's experimental methodology and porosity/geometry-based approach to characterizing volumetric absorber performance (efficiency, outlet temperature, flux, absorption depth) against baseline metallic/ceramic receivers provides a directly comparable experimental framework for characterizing an installed SiC honeycomb receiver's absorption and thermal performance under concentrated solar flux.

Avila_Marin_Fernandez_Reche_2022_Experim.title: Experimental study of innovative periodic cellular structures as air volumetric absorbers
Avila_Marin_Fernandez_Reche_2022_Experim.system: Five novel periodic/non-periodic SiC porous morphologies (diamond, rotated cube, tetrakaidecahedron, cube shifted, Voronoi) as open volumetric solar air absorbers, compared against conventional SiC honeycomb and random foam absorbers.
Avila_Marin_Fernandez_Reche_2022_Experim.method: Lab-scale solar simulator experimental thermal evaluation of absorber samples, including constant and gradually-varying cell-size configurations, benchmarked against honeycomb and foam references.
findings: Voronoi morphology, both with constant cell size and with an increasing cell size pattern, achieved a performance gain over the conventional SiC honeycomb and random foam absorbers.
Reference literature cited: Capuano's staggered-honeycomb pin design increased thermal efficiency by 12% versus the HiTRec baseline ceramic absorber.

Pabst et al.'s scaled-up samples (54 cups, 18 per sample) tested at Jülich Solar Tower achieved ~800°C air outlet temperatures with ~80% thermal efficiency, improving overall receiver performance by 5%.
Wang's SiC foam study found the sample with highest specific surface area (1328 m⁻¹), 66% porosity and 40 PPI performed best among four porosities (65-70-75-85%) and three pore sizes (15-20-40 PPI).

Patil et al. reported designs exceeding 1000°C outlet temperature with ~65% thermal efficiency using 10-30 PPI porous materials at 0.90 porosity, 1965-3900 suns concentration, and 2-10 kg/h air mass flow.
Avila_Marin_Fernandez_Reche_2022_Experim.validation_data: Experimental thermal efficiency and air outlet temperature measurements from solar-simulator testing of the sample absorbers, compared against reference honeycomb and random foam absorber results.
Avila_Marin_Fernandez_Reche_2022_Experim.limitations_stated: Luque's recent work found that the theoretical benefit of a volumetric effect over a novel additively manufactured volumetric absorber was not observed; Mey et al. noted that among foams tested, smallest pore diameter and lowest porosity gave best results, indicating morphology-dependent performance not yet generalized.
Avila_Marin_Fernandez_Reche_2022_Experim.relevance: Provides direct experimental thermal-efficiency benchmarking methodology and comparison data for SiC honeycomb and novel cellular absorber morphologies under concentrated solar flux, relevant context for characterizing an installed SiC honeycomb receiver's performance against alternative structures.

C2_060_Haseler_Ali_2021_Machine_Learning.title: Positioning and focusing of light sources in light concentrating systems using convolutional neural network modelling
C2_060_Haseler_Ali_2021_Machine_Learning.system: A 7-lamp (6 kW Xe short-arc) high flux solar simulator (HFSS) at Texas A&M at Qatar, with a Lambertian target and heat flux gauge, used to develop a CNN that predicts the relative x, y, z position of the light source from illuminated-target images.
C2_060_Haseler_Ali_2021_Machine_Learning.method: Flux characterization (radiometer measurements correlated with HDR-SR processed CCD grayscale images) established a baseline human-operator positioning accuracy, and Monte Carlo ray tracing (TracePro) generated over 2,500 virtual flux-map images used to train and validate a convolutional neural network predicting light-source position.
findings: The mechanical slider system had a calculated resolution of 0.06 mm, but measured (precision micrometer) resolution of about 0.14 mm per axis, corresponding to a Euclidean positioning accuracy |d|HFSS of about 0.24 mm.

The CNN predicted light source position within 0.07, 0.11, and 0.07 mm in the x-, y-, and z-directions respectively, i.e. a Euclidean distance of ~0.249 mm, comparable to the mechanical system's ~0.24 mm accuracy.

Flux-irradiance vs normalized image irradiance correlations gave NRMSE ≈ 0.86 for a linear fit (slope a = 1186.4 W/m^2) and NRMSE ≈ 0.89 for a power-law fit (a = 1117.5 W/m^2, exponent b = 0.903); the power-law form was selected for further use.
Gaussian fits to the flux profile validated the focused-light Gaussian distribution with NRMSE ~0.07 (x-axis) and ~0.12 (y-axis).
The Lambertian target 3-axis slider had a resolution of 0.08 μm and 1 μm repeatability, and the calibrated heat flux gauge had 1% repeatability and ±3% transducer calibration accuracy.
C2_060_Haseler_Ali_2021_Machine_Learning.validation_data: Radiometer (Gardon-type heat flux gauge) flux measurements calibrated against a NIST-traceable sensor, combined with CCD camera grayscale images of a Lambertian target, were used to build irradiance-vs-image correlations (linear and power-law) and Gaussian flux profile fits; these experimental flux maps and the measured mechanical positioning accuracy (0.24 mm) served as the baseline/validation metrics for the CNN's predicted source position accuracy.
C2_060_Haseler_Ali_2021_Machine_Learning.limitations_stated: The as-built CAD model of the lamp was overly complex (millions of triangular elements), substantially slowing simulations; experimental flux data showed a tail at high irradiance levels attributed to control-system malfunction, which was retained to show its minor effect on large-dataset calibration; the heat flux gauge required calorimetric recalibration to account for spectral differences between the calibration blackbody source and the actual lamp spectrum.
C2_060_Haseler_Ali_2021_Machine_Learning.relevance: The paper's rigorous experimental flux characterization methodology (radiometer calibration, HDR-SR imaging, Gaussian flux mapping, and quantified positioning/measurement uncertainties) illustrates techniques and accuracy benchmarks relevant to characterizing the incident flux distribution on an installed SiC honeycomb receiver in a solar simulator or solar tower setup, though it does not address heat transfer within a porous/honeycomb absorber itself.

C2_063_Tayseir_2022_Solar_DRR.title: Optical and experimental evaluation of a directly irradiated solar reactor for the catalytic dry reforming of methane
C2_063_Tayseir_2022_Solar_DRR.system: A tubular, transparent-walled (quartz) solar reactor directly irradiating a Ni-based catalytic fixed bed (20% Ni on Al2O3) for dry reforming of methane, driven by a ~3 kW high flux solar simulator.
C2_063_Tayseir_2022_Solar_DRR.method: Monte-Carlo ray-tracing optical modeling was used to design the reactor and estimate irradiance distribution, followed by experimental testing of methane/CO2 conversion and syngas quality at three temperatures and several gas hourly space velocities.
findings: Methane conversion ranged from ~53% at 550°C to ~93% at 800°C.
H2/CO ratio ranged from ~0.4 at 550°C to ~0.9 at 800°C.
GHSV values tested were around 17–58 l h-1 g-1 (corresponding to GHSV of 865, 1270, and 2900 h-1).
Quartz reactor walls showed no degradation after more than 80 h of intermittent testing.

Overall light-to-chemical energy efficiency was less than 1% based on radiation intercepted by the whole reactor system, rising to 5%–25% when corrected for the actual irradiance reaching the catalytic bed.
C2_063_Tayseir_2022_Solar_DRR.validation_data: Experimental irradiance measurements on the reactor aperture and catalytic bed (from the optical/ray-tracing model), and measured methane conversion and H2/CO ratios compared against literature values for the same Ni-based catalyst.
C2_063_Tayseir_2022_Solar_DRR.limitations_stated: The non-uniform distribution of irradiance on the catalytic bed limits performance and lowers the overall light-to-chemical efficiency to below 1% when based on total radiation intercepted by the reactor system (improving to 5–25% only after correcting for the actual irradiance reaching the bed); the work is described as preliminary experimental and numerical findings.
C2_063_Tayseir_2022_Solar_DRR.relevance: Provides an example methodology—combining Monte-Carlo ray-tracing irradiance modeling with experimental flux/performance characterization of a directly irradiated catalytic absorber—that parallels the optical and thermal characterization needs of an installed, directly irradiated SiC honeycomb receiver, though it does not address internal convective heat transfer or Nusselt-type correlations within the honeycomb channels.

C2_065_Fathya_2023_Solar_Receiver.title: Exploring and enhancing the volumetric behaviour in solar receivers through specular reflectivity and simplified design
C2_065_Fathya_2023_Solar_Receiver.system: A single-channel square-channel honeycomb volumetric solar receiver (modelled after HiTRec-II geometry) irradiated by a four-lamp-block High Flux Solar Simulator, with varied surface reflectivity (diffuse and specular) along the channel walls.
C2_065_Fathya_2023_Solar_Receiver.method: A 3D steady-state mathematical model coupling conduction, convection and radiation (source term obtained via Monte-Carlo Ray Tracing) was developed for a single repeating channel unit, verified against literature experimental data, and used in a parametric study of reflectivity distributions.
findings: Diffuse reflectivity distributions improved thermal efficiency but did not enhance radiation penetration.
The improved specular-reflectivity receiver achieved a thermal efficiency of 96%, compared to 85% for the commercial HiTRec-II receiver.
In the literature SolAir-200-based model, 90% of radiation was absorbed in the front 20% of the receiver.
Specular reflectivity produced a more uniform source term distribution, enabling the receiver to be classified as a true volumetric receiver.
C2_065_Fathya_2023_Solar_Receiver.ltne: not considered (single-channel solid/gas heat transfer treated via convection/HTC in the 3D model, but no explicit local thermal non-equilibrium correlation or magnitude is reported in the extracted text)
C2_065_Fathya_2023_Solar_Receiver.validation_data: Model veracity was confirmed against existing literature experimental data (incident flux of 650 kW/m2 and DLR HFSS lamp block configuration/dimensions from Alxneit et al., used to match the literature verification case).
C2_065_Fathya_2023_Solar_Receiver.limitations_stated: Prior graded-porosity/fractal-like designs demonstrating the volumetric effect require layered manufacturing techniques compatible only with metals, prohibiting use of high-performance ceramics; packed-bed/coated approaches to improve radiation penetration do not eliminate design complexity or, in some cases, fail to report achieving the volumetric effect.
C2_065_Fathya_2023_Solar_Receiver.relevance: The paper's 3D single-channel honeycomb model, MCRT-derived source term, and thermal efficiency/volumetric-effect metrics provide a modelling and definitional framework directly applicable to interpreting axial temperature and efficiency data from an installed SiC honeycomb receiver characterization.

Capuano_Fend_et_al_2016_Numerical_models.title: Numerical models of advanced ceramic absorbers for volumetric solar receivers
Capuano_Fend_et_al_2016_Numerical_models.system: Volumetric solar air receivers with ceramic (SiC-type) porous absorbers used in solar tower plants, comparing several DLR-developed numerical models against a reference experimental case.
Capuano_Fend_et_al_2016_Numerical_models.method: Overview and re-running/comparison of existing discrete (one-dimensional, one-channel, quasi-3D analytical, single-channel discrete) and continuum (homogeneous porous medium) numerical models against pre-existing experimental data, using outlet temperature, absorbed heat and efficiency as comparison metrics.
findings: Predicted outlet air temperatures were 1050 K (Pitz-Paal model), 1048 K (Hoffschmidt model), 1057 K (Fend & Smirnova single-channel), and 1073 K (Fend & Smirnova continuum), versus 972 K measured experimentally.
Absorbed fluid heat QAbs.fl. was 1.90, 1.89, 1.92 and 1.96 W for the four models respectively, versus 1.69 W experimentally.
Predicted efficiencies were 0.78, 0.77, 0.79 and 0.81 for the four models respectively, versus 0.69 measured experimentally.
The HiTRec receiver's recrystallized SiC honeycomb absorber had an open porosity of 49.5%, arranged in 37 hexagonal modules with SiSiC cups.
The Phoebus-TSA metallic volumetric receiver (2.5 MWth) achieved 85% efficiency at an average flux of 0.3 MW/m2, producing steam at 500 °C with a stabilized outlet air temperature of 700 °C.
Capuano_Fend_et_al_2016_Numerical_models.nu_correlation: Churchill et al. correlation for tubes in cross flow used at the channel inlet in Becker et al.'s 1D model: Nu = 0.3 + [0.62 Re^0.5 Pr^(1/3) / (1+(0.4/Pr)^(2/3))^(1/4)] * [1+(Re/28200)^(5/8)]^(4/5), valid for Re between 10^2 and 10^7 and Pe > 0.2; wall thickness b used as characteristic length in Re.
Capuano_Fend_et_al_2016_Numerical_models.ltne: Local thermal non-equilibrium between solid and fluid phases is treated implicitly by presenting separate solid and fluid temperature profiles (Fig. 9, 'Mean temperature profiles of solid and fluid phase') in most discrete/analytical models, i.e. assumed/modeled as non-equilibrium; however Roldán et al. (cited) is noted to consider thermal equilibrium between solid and fluid phases instead. No explicit magnitude of the temperature gap between phases is given in the extracted text.
Capuano_Fend_et_al_2016_Numerical_models.validation_data: Experimental outlet air temperature (Toutlet = 972 K), absorbed heat content in air (QAbs.fl. = 1.69 W) and receiver efficiency (η = 0.69) from a pre-existing experimental evaluation are used as reference/validation values against which the numerical models are compared.
Capuano_Fend_et_al_2016_Numerical_models.limitations_stated: The authors state a substantial gap between numerical and experimental results, attributed to variable environmental conditions, difficulty in experimentally evaluating mean air flow temperature (e.g., thermocouple placement issues and hard-to-assess flow losses), and inadequate representation of radiative heat exchange in the models; this gap is more pronounced for the continuum approach due to added approximation from homogeneous representation; discrete models are also limited by heavy computational cost from detailed porous-volume representation.
Capuano_Fend_et_al_2016_Numerical_models.relevance: The paper's direct comparison of multiple numerical absorber models against a real ceramic honeycomb receiver's measured outlet temperature, absorbed heat and efficiency—and its identification of radiative heat transfer characterization and flow-temperature measurement uncertainty as key error sources—provides directly applicable benchmarking context and caveats for interpreting experimental characterization of an installed SiC honeycomb receiver.

Cornejo_Hayes_2020_Nu_Number_Correlation.title: Improved Nu number correlations for gas flow in monolith reactors using temperature-dependent fluid properties
Cornejo_Hayes_2020_Nu_Number_Correlation.system: Laminar gas (air) flow and convective heat/mass transfer inside single circular monolith honeycomb channels, modelled with three inlet geometries (straight, reservoir, contraction) under constant wall temperature or constant wall heat flux boundary conditions.
Cornejo_Hayes_2020_Nu_Number_Correlation.method: Detailed 2D axisymmetric CFD (ANSYS Fluent v18.2) computational experiments across a range of channel Reynolds numbers, void fractions and heating rates, comparing constant vs. temperature-dependent fluid properties (density from ideal gas law, viscosity/conductivity from kinetic theory, Cp from polynomial fits) and fitting a new Nu vs. inverse Graetz number correlation.
findings: Channel Re ranged from 50 to 600 and heating rate (tau = Tmax/Tmin) from 1.1 to 3.0 across 38 computational runs.
Using inlet temperature instead of local temperature to compute RePr (Peclet number) introduces errors as high as 50% or more, shifting the apparent Nu vs. 1/Gz curve.

At constant wall temperature and high heating rate, a minimum appears in the Nu vs. 1/Gz curve about 16% below the asymptotic value for tau = 2; the minimum's placement and value are not significantly affected by Re.
At constant wall heat flux, the minimum Nu decreases only slightly with increasing heat flux H and remains comparable to (negligibly different from) the asymptotic value.

Grid independence confirmed with meshes of 492,164 and 1,968,656 quadrilateral cells (80 and 160 radial elements); the coarser 492,164-cell mesh (channel diameter D=1 mm, length L=75 mm) was used throughout and matched literature fully-developed Nu (Kays and Crawford; Bhatti solution).
Cornejo_Hayes_2020_Nu_Number_Correlation.nu_correlation: Classical form Nu = Nu_inf[1 + B(Gz)^n exp(-C/Gz)] (and analogous Sh form) is reviewed as inadequate when a minimum occurs; a novel correlation combining this classical form with a sigmoid function is proposed to fit Nu vs. 1/Gz across entrance, minimum, and asymptotic regions, calibrated via a fitting methodology, with empirical sub-models for the value and axial placement of the minimum Nu expressed as functions of heating rate tau only, valid for channel Re 50-600.
Cornejo_Hayes_2020_Nu_Number_Correlation.ltne: Not considered — the study treats only single-phase gas flow with a specified wall temperature or wall heat flux boundary condition (fluid-solid coupling via Nu correlations is the topic, but no separate solid-phase temperature field or thermal non-equilibrium magnitude between phases is computed).
Cornejo_Hayes_2020_Nu_Number_Correlation.validation_data: Grid-independence and validation performed by comparing computed Nu vs. 1/Gz curves (constant wall temperature, low heating rate, straight channel with flat inlet velocity profile) against literature fully-developed Nu values for circular pipes (Kays and Crawford) and the Bhatti analytical solution for constant fluid properties.
Cornejo_Hayes_2020_Nu_Number_Correlation.limitations_stated: Flow was assumed laminar (upstream turbulence effects deferred to a future investigation); fluid properties studies mentioned in literature that vary properties one at a time are called non-physical; the new empirical Nu model requires a relatively large number of empirical parameters, and the authors recommend a statistical sensitivity analysis and potential model reduction as further work; results are limited to circular cross-section channels and air-like gases with Pr close to 0.7.
Cornejo_Hayes_2020_Nu_Number_Correlation.relevance: Provides quantitative Nu correlations and identifies key errors (up to 50% from reference-temperature choice, and a distinct sub-asymptotic Nu minimum at high heating rates) relevant to selecting or validating heat-transfer coefficients for lumped/porous-medium models of an installed SiC honeycomb receiver operating under large temperature gradients and high heating rates.

Cui_Kaer_2018_Two_dimensional_thermal_an.title: Two-dimensional thermal analysis of radial heat transfer of monoliths in small-scale steam methane reforming
Cui_Kaer_2018_Two_dimensional_thermal_an.system: Radial heat transfer behavior of monolithic (honeycomb) catalyst substrates used in small-scale steam methane reforming reactors, with and without endothermic reaction, washcoat, and wall gap effects.
Cui_Kaer_2018_Two_dimensional_thermal_an.method: Two-dimensional CFD simulations (ANSYS FLUENT 18.0) of one-eighth symmetric monolith cross-sections, using DO and S2S radiation models and a pseudo-continuous/pseudo-homogeneous symmetric model, parametrically varying substrate thermal conductivity, washcoat, wall gap, cell density, porosity, and diameter.
findings: The effective radial thermal conductivity (kr,eff) predicted by CFD showed good agreement with the pseudo-continuous symmetric model.
A wall gap as thin as 0.05 mm significantly decreased kr,eff, while radiation heat transfer only showed limited improvement in compensating for it.
The influence of radiation heat transfer on kr,eff is low for highly conductive monoliths (e.g., substrates with conductivity around 16 W/m·K or higher).

Reference reaction heat Qwash,ref was set to 3.6×10^7 W/m3 (equivalent to 3.6×10^9 W/m3 with virtual washcoat thickness of 0.3 mm), derived from industrial packed-bed SMR data (90 kW/m2 tube wall heat flux, 0.1 catalyst effectiveness factor, 0.5 porosity, 200 mm tube diameter).
Highly conductive substrates such as Ni (71 W/m·K) and SiC (350 W/m·K) showed the greatest potential for intensifying the steam reforming process compared to FeCralloy (16 W/m·K).
Cui_Kaer_2018_Two_dimensional_thermal_an.ltne: not considered (the model used a pseudo-homogeneous/pseudo-continuous single-temperature-field 2D conduction formulation for radial heat transfer; gas phase was treated as static/conductive only, not as a separate thermally non-equilibrated phase)
Cui_Kaer_2018_Two_dimensional_thermal_an.validation_data: CFD-predicted effective radial thermal conductivity (kr,eff) was compared against predictions from the pseudo-continuous symmetric model (Groppi/Tronconi-type analytical model) for validation; reaction heat source was calibrated against industrial-scale packed-bed SMR reference data (tube wall heat flux, catalyst effectiveness factor, porosity, tube diameter).
Cui_Kaer_2018_Two_dimensional_thermal_an.limitations_stated: Gas phase was assumed static (no flow effects on radial heat transfer); thermal conductivity of substrate and gas assumed temperature-independent (valid only within ~5% for <100 K differences for stainless steel/nickel); axial heat/mass transfer and detailed SMR kinetics not included; uniform catalyst activity assumed; height of monolith arbitrarily set to 1 m for volumetric heat transfer rate calculation; variation of gap resistance at different positions in the reformer not considered.
Cui_Kaer_2018_Two_dimensional_thermal_an.relevance: The paper's CFD-derived correlations and G-factor model for effective radial thermal conductivity, radiation contribution, and wall-gap sensitivity in high-conductivity (including SiC) honeycomb monoliths provide a modeling framework and quantitative benchmarks (e.g., wall-gap sensitivity, radiation contribution thresholds) against which measured radial temperature/heat-flux data from an installed SiC honeycomb receiver could be compared or validated.

Fend_2013_Numerical_investigation_offlow.title: Numerical investigation of flow and heat transfer in a volumetric solar receiver
Fend_2013_Numerical_investigation_offlow.system: An extruded Silicon Carbide honeycomb volumetric solar receiver (140x140 mm module, based on the Jülich Solar Tower design) exposed to concentrated radiation from Xenon short-arc lamps, studying the effect of channel/wall geometry and overall absorber shape (with/without frustum) on temperature distribution and solar-to-thermal efficiency.
Fend_2013_Numerical_investigation_offlow.method: Two 3D COMSOL Multiphysics numerical models (a single-channel model resolving real honeycomb channel geometry, and a continuum model treating the absorber as a homogenized porous medium with a two-equation solid/fluid heat transfer term) were developed and compared against experimental data from a tubular solar-simulator test rig using Xenon short-arc lamps and water/air enthalpy-balance efficiency measurements.
findings: Air heats from 40°C to more than 750°C passing through the standard-geometry channel, with the temperature profile becoming constant after approximately 20 mm from the inlet.
Average difference between simulated and measured outlet temperatures and thermal efficiency was approximately 1-2%.

Two channel geometries tested: Sample 1 (2.18 mm channel width, 0.55 mm wall thickness, 1170 m2/m3 specific surface) and Sample 2 (1.43 mm channel width, 0.25 mm wall thickness, 2027 m2/m3 specific surface), both under 650 kW/m2 incident flux.
The absorber with smaller channels (higher specific surface) shows lower front temperatures and faster air temperature rise due to increased surface area and lower convective heat resistance.

Radiation attenuation in the cellular material follows an exponential law with an experimentally determined extinction coefficient of 2300 1/m; the frustum geometry produces a homogeneous inlet temperature distribution versus a non-homogeneous one without frustum, attributed to lower mass flow near the cup walls.
Fend_2013_Numerical_investigation_offlow.ltne: assumed - two separate energy equations are solved simultaneously for the gaseous and solid phases in both the single-channel and continuum models, coupled via a volumetric convective exchange term q' = a·AV·(T2 - T); the volumetric heat transfer coefficient (a·AV) was derived from the single-channel model's numerical heat flow distribution and specific surface AV, no explicit magnitude value given in this excerpt.
Fend_2013_Numerical_investigation_offlow.validation_data: Average solar heat flux (650 kW/m2, with experimental range 300-700 kW/m2), mass flow rate, inlet air temperature, measured air outlet temperature, extinction coefficient (from transmittance measurements), permeability and effective heat conductivity (experimentally determined), and solar-to-thermal efficiency (from water-circuit enthalpy balance).
Fend_2013_Numerical_investigation_offlow.limitations_stated: The single-channel model requires a high number of elements due to complex geometry and thus can only be applied to a small excerpt of the total receiver volume, not the whole component of more than 2000 channels; heat transfer at the outer surface of the cup was neglected in the continuum model to simplify it.
Fend_2013_Numerical_investigation_offlow.relevance: Provides a validated dual-modeling framework (single-channel and porous-continuum with LTNE coupling) and experimental efficiency/outlet-temperature benchmarking methodology directly applicable to characterizing an installed SiC honeycomb receiver's flow, temperature distribution, and volumetric heat transfer performance under concentrated solar flux.

Fend_Hoffschmidt_2004_Porous_materials_a.title: Porous materials as open volumetric solar receivers: Experimental determination of thermophysical and heat transfer properties
Fend_Hoffschmidt_2004_Porous_materials_a.system: Various porous absorber materials (ceramic foams of cordierite, SSiC and CBSiC at 10/20/45 ppi, SiC fibre mesh, SiC and metallic catalyst carriers, and combined material systems) intended for use as open volumetric solar receivers.
Fend_Hoffschmidt_2004_Porous_materials_a.method: Thermal conductivity was measured with the transient hot-disk technique, convective heat transfer coefficient (as the product a·AV) was measured using a temperature-wave phase-shift/attenuation method in an air flow rig, flow instability was studied via infrared imaging of front-surface cooling after a step change in flow velocity, and efficiency was measured in the DLR Solar Furnace with an isolated test bed and water heat exchanger.
findings: Fibre mesh plus SiC catalyst carrier combined receiver reached efficiencies of 75–92% at air outlet temperatures of 300–550°C, higher than the fibre mesh alone.

For metallic catalyst carriers, the 1600 cpsi material achieved 2–3% higher efficiency than the 800 cpsi material, with average outlet temperature limited to 400°C to avoid peak temperatures over 1000°C.

Ceramic foam heat conductivities varied strongly with wall material: SSiC 45 ppi ~2.7 W/mK, CBSiC 45 ppi ~0.6 W/mK, cordierite 20 ppi ~0.2 W/mK (bulk wall conductivities: cordierite ~1 W/mK, CBSiC ~10 W/mK, SSiC ~100 W/mK).

45 ppi foams showed significantly higher heat transfer coefficient × specific surface (AV·a) than 10/20 ppi foams due to higher specific surface (up to 2500 m2/m3 vs 500–1000 m2/m3), with the effect more pronounced for CBSiC than SSiC, attributed to closed pores in SSiC.

SiC catalyst carrier (2 mm channel, 0.8 mm wall) reached air outlet temperatures over 1000°C and withstands up to 1600°C, but has limited efficiency potential due to minor heat transfer in the front area causing high front temperatures.

Cordierite foam (20 ppi) showed rapid compensation of front temperature inhomogeneities during cooling, whereas a cordierite catalyst carrier (400 cpsi) showed a permanent inhomogeneous temperature distribution despite similar bulk thermophysical properties.
Fend_Hoffschmidt_2004_Porous_materials_a.nu_correlation: No explicit Nusselt correlation given; instead the product of heat transfer coefficient and specific surface (AV·a) is reported as a function of Reynolds number (Re = vPore·ρ·dH/g, with vPore = v/P0 and dH derived from porosity and pore size s = 0.0254/(1.5·nPPI)) for SSiC, CBSiC and cordierite foams (10/20/45 ppi), showing AV·a increasing with Re and with higher ppi (higher specific surface).
Fend_Hoffschmidt_2004_Porous_materials_a.validation_data: Air inlet/outlet temperature and mass flow measurements (for efficiency), phase shift and attenuation of an imposed temperature wave through the sample (for AV·a heat transfer measurement), and hot-disk temperature-rise curves (for thermal conductivity/diffusivity) are used to derive/calibrate the reported thermophysical and heat-transfer quantities; infrared surface temperature maps are used to characterize flow/temperature homogeneity.
Fend_Hoffschmidt_2004_Porous_materials_a.limitations_stated: The SiC catalyst carrier's channel/wall geometry leads to minor heat transfer in the front area and relatively high front temperatures, limiting efficiency potential; metallic catalyst carriers required outlet temperature to be capped at 400°C to prevent peak temperatures exceeding 1000°C due to inhomogeneous flow/temperature distribution; the modified 800 cpsi material with channel narrowing showed only a slight improvement and the narrowing was 'not as distinctive as necessary,' requiring further samples to be manufactured.
Fend_Hoffschmidt_2004_Porous_materials_a.relevance: The paper provides directly comparable experimental methods and material-property data (specific surface, wall/pore heat conductivity, and AV·a vs Reynolds number) for SiC-based catalyst-carrier and foam absorbers, including a HELIOTECH SiC parallel-channel monolith previously used in the SOLAIR project, offering a benchmark and measurement methodology relevant to characterizing an installed SiC honeycomb receiver's heat transfer and flow-homogeneity performance.

Fend_Pitz_Paal_et_al_2004_Two_novel_high.title: Two novel high-porosity materials as volumetric receivers for concentrated solar radiation
Fend_Pitz_Paal_et_al_2004_Two_novel_high.system: Two novel porous silicon carbide volumetric receiver materials (a double-layer SiC foam and a screen-printed/Direct-Typing-Process porous SiC material) tested as absorbers for concentrated solar radiation in solar tower technology.
Fend_Pitz_Paal_et_al_2004_Two_novel_high.method: Pressure-loss (permeability) measurements over 0–6 m/s air velocity and solar furnace efficiency tests at the DLR Solar Furnace, monitoring DNI, front (peak) temperature by pyrometer, air outlet and heat-exchanger temperatures, air and water mass flows, optical flux via camera/target method, and front temperature distribution via infrared camera.
findings: The 80/20 ppi double-layer foam sample (Ø70 mm) reached efficiencies up to 98% at POA/AMF ~655 kJ/kg, with air outlet temperatures up to 672°C and material front temperatures up to 867°C.
The single-layer 20 ppi foam sample (Ø80 mm) reached efficiencies up to 94% at POA/AMF ~636 kJ/kg, with air outlet temperatures up to 663°C and front temperatures up to 803°C.

For the Direct-Typing-Process material, efficiency was roughly estimated at 80% at 2.3 kW power on aperture, with average air outlet temperature up to 650°C and peak front temperatures of about 1200°C under a Gaussian flux ranging from 0.5 MW/m2 (center) to 0.15 MW/m2 (edges).
Estimated heat losses through the 20 cm insulation layer were below 2% at 800°C air temperature after at least 30 min of continuous insolation.
Stated measurement accuracies: pressure-loss measurements ~±5%, POA (camera/target) measurement ~±3.5%, overall efficiency measurement accuracy ~±4.8%.
Fend_Pitz_Paal_et_al_2004_Two_novel_high.validation_data: Efficiency test data (DNI, aperture power, air/water mass flows, inlet/outlet air and water temperatures, front temperature via pyrometer/IR camera, optical flux via camera/target method) were used to compute receiver efficiency and are compared against previously published data for wire-mesh, SiC catalyst carrier, and metallic parallel-channel (800 cpsi) receiver materials.
Fend_Pitz_Paal_et_al_2004_Two_novel_high.limitations_stated: Efficiency accuracy limited to ±4.8% due to combined temperature, mass-flow and optical flux measurement uncertainties; tube insulation heat losses (<2% at 800°C) not fully eliminated; Direct-Typing-Process material efficiency was only roughly estimated due to short measurement duration and strong fluctuation of incident solar power from weather conditions; future work must address long-term high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance.
Fend_Pitz_Paal_et_al_2004_Two_novel_high.relevance: Establishes the solar-furnace efficiency testing methodology (flux, temperature, mass-flow measurements and efficiency/POA-per-mass-flow analysis) and benchmark performance data for porous SiC volumetric receivers, providing a direct precedent and comparative baseline for experimentally characterizing an installed SiC honeycomb receiver.

Filho_2020_thermal_radiation_porous_medi.title: An Analysis of Thermal Radiation in Porous Media Under Local Thermal Non-equilibrium
Filho_2020_thermal_radiation_porous_medi.system: Forced convection and radiative heat transfer in a two-dimensional channel and a cylindrical (tube) geometry filled with porous media under local thermal non-equilibrium, representative of high-temperature combustion/porous burner conditions.
Filho_2020_thermal_radiation_porous_medi.method: Macroscopic volume-averaged continuity, momentum and two-energy (solid/fluid) equations are solved numerically with the finite volume method, with the radiative transfer equation solved via the discrete ordinate method (DOM) and finite volume method (FVM), compared against a Rosseland diffusion approximation and a non-radiative model, including a sensitivity study on absorption/scattering coefficients and extinction coefficient effects on the Nusselt number.
findings: Temperatures from the Rosseland model differ by up to +34% and -26% compared to DOM/FVM radiation calculations.

The maximum difference between the Rosseland model and the R.T.E. (DOM/FVM) solved fields was 75.98%, showing the Rosseland model can give very different results, especially failing near boundaries and in pipes/channels with high wall heat flux.

Perturbing absorption and scattering coefficients by ±50% caused a maximum temperature field difference of 3.32% for isotropic scattering cases, and up to 6.17% for cases with absorption/emission but no scattering.

For the extinction coefficient β between 0 and 200, the Nusselt number decreased with increasing β; for β > 200, Nusselt number increased with increasing β, with the maximum Nusselt number obtained using the non-radiative model (i.e., at the limits of very low or very high β).
DOM and FVM temperature fields are very similar, with significant differences only appearing when a very low number of angular directions is used.
Filho_2020_thermal_radiation_porous_medi.nu_correlation: Two literature correlations are used/adopted for interfacial/volumetric heat transfer: Fu et al. (1998) volumetric Nusselt correlation Nu_v = h_v d_m^2 / k_f = C Re^m (from inverse method on five ceramics); Kuwahara et al. (2001) correlation Nu = hD/k_f = (1 + 4(1-ϕ)/ϕ) + (1/2)(1-ϕ)^{1/2} Re_D^{0.6} Pr^{1/3}, valid for 0.2<ϕ<0.9, Re from 10^-2 to 10^3, Pr from 10^-2 to 10^2 — the latter is the one adopted in the present simulations. Additionally, the paper examines how the local Nusselt number varies with extinction coefficient β (decreasing for 0<β<200, increasing for β>200).
Filho_2020_thermal_radiation_porous_medi.ltne: Assumed/modeled: local thermal non-equilibrium is explicitly adopted via a two-energy-equation model (separate solid- and fluid-phase energy equations coupled through a volumetric heat transfer coefficient h_v), not measured experimentally; magnitude of solid-fluid temperature differences is examined via the coupled energy equations and Nusselt-number/extinction-coefficient sensitivity, but no single non-equilibrium magnitude value is reported.
Filho_2020_thermal_radiation_porous_medi.validation_data: Permeability values from Petrasch et al. (2007) direct pore-level simulation and the Kuwahara et al. (1998) correlation; the adopted convective heat transfer correlation (Kuwahara et al. 2001) was validated against experimental packed-bed data of Wakao and Kagei (1982). No new experimental data were generated in this paper itself.
Filho_2020_thermal_radiation_porous_medi.limitations_stated: The Rosseland diffusion approximation is not valid near boundaries and fails in pipes/channels with high wall heat flux; permeability from Kuwahara et al. (1998) is a simplified-geometry correlation that gives higher pressure drop than Petrasch et al. (2007) DPLS values tied to a specific sample; dispersion and tortuosity effects are neglected in the effective conductivity tensors; the fluid phase is assumed transparent to radiation and the solid phase is assumed gray.
Filho_2020_thermal_radiation_porous_medi.relevance: The paper's two-energy-equation LTNE framework, radiative transfer solution methods (DOM/FVM vs. Rosseland), and Nusselt-number/extinction-coefficient sensitivity results provide modeling context and correlation comparisons relevant to interpreting solid- and fluid-phase temperature differences and effective heat transfer coefficients in an experimentally characterized SiC honeycomb receiver operating under combined radiation-convection-conduction with potential local thermal non-equilibrium.

Hayes_2009_effective_thermal_conductivit.title: The effective thermal conductivity of monolith honeycomb structures
Hayes_2009_effective_thermal_conductivit.system: Monolith honeycomb structures (square, triangular, hexagonal cells, with and without washcoat) used to determine effective axial and radial thermal conductivity for continuum reactor models.
Hayes_2009_effective_thermal_conductivit.method: Analytical network (series/parallel electrical resistance) models were derived for effective axial and radial thermal conductivity and compared against 2D finite-element numerical solutions (COMSOL Multiphysics 3.5a) of the discretized fluid/substrate/washcoat domains, including single-cell rows and quarter-circle 'web' domains.
findings: For a blank square-cell monolith of 75% porosity, the G factor approaches an asymptotic limit of 0.134 as solid thermal conductivity increases beyond about kS = 10 W/(m K), and approaches unity as kS approaches the fluid conductivity.
A Cordierite monolith (kS = 1.5 W/(m K), 75% porosity) has an effective thermal conductivity of about 0.25 W/(m K), versus about 0.75 W/(m K) for a steel monolith (kS = 15 W/(m K), 93% porosity).
For a 75% porosity substrate with 10% washcoat added (porosity drops to 56.8%), a circular (fillet) washcoat shape gives a G value about 3% higher than uniformly distributed washcoat of equal volume.
Using the 2D 'web' domain versus a 4-cell row model, G is essentially identical at 75% porosity but about 4% higher via the web model at 61% porosity.

Among uncoated 75%-porosity cell shapes, triangular and square cells have very similar effective thermal conductivities, while hexagonal cells give the lowest; adding 10% washcoat increases G in all cases, most for fillet-shaped washcoat, with the triangular cell plus non-uniform (fillet) washcoat giving the highest overall effective conductivity.
Hayes_2009_effective_thermal_conductivit.ltne: assumed: a two-equation heterogeneous model (Eqs. 1-2) with a volumetric heat transfer coefficient h and area av coupling fluid and solid temperatures is presented as the standard heterogeneous approach, but no magnitude of thermal non-equilibrium or h value is given; the paper's own analysis focuses on conduction (effective thermal conductivity) rather than fluid-solid heat exchange.
Hayes_2009_effective_thermal_conductivit.validation_data: No experimental data are used; the analytical (series/parallel network) models are validated against 2D finite-element numerical solutions of the fully discretized fluid/substrate/washcoat conduction problem, using computed heat flux and back-calculated effective conductivity (Eq. 27) as the reference.
Hayes_2009_effective_thermal_conductivit.limitations_stated: The electrical network analogy assumes one-dimensional heat transfer and is therefore not exact, since actual conduction in the monolith is multi-dimensional; the parallel model generally outperforms the series model but the true value lies between the two; results also depend on unmodeled orientation effects and idealized (uniform vs. fillet) washcoat shape assumptions.
Hayes_2009_effective_thermal_conductivit.relevance: The derived effective radial/axial thermal conductivity models and the finding that conduction is bracketed by series/parallel limits and sensitive to porosity, washcoat distribution, and cell shape provide a framework for estimating the effective solid-phase conductivity of an installed SiC honeycomb receiver needed to interpret its measured transient/steady-state thermal response.

Hayes_2021_Multi_scale_modelling_of_mono.title: Multi-scale modelling of monolith reactors: A 30-year perspective from 1990 to 2020
Hayes_2021_Multi_scale_modelling_of_mono.journal: The Canadian Journal of Chemical Engineering
Hayes_2021_Multi_scale_modelling_of_mono.system: Honeycomb-type monolith reactors used in catalytic automotive exhaust gas after-treatment and related catalytic processes, covering single-channel and full-reactor scales.
Hayes_2021_Multi_scale_modelling_of_mono.method: Historical/narrative review of 30 years of the authors' computational modelling work (finite element method and later commercial CFD software such as FEMLAB/COMSOL and Fluent) on momentum, mass, heat transfer and radiation in monolith channels.
findings: The multi-scale nature of the monolith problem spans at least seven orders of magnitude, from washcoat pores (~10 nm) to reactor diameters of tens of centimetres.
Typical washcoat thickness ranges from 10-150 microns depending on channel shape and coating method, with channel hydraulic diameter on the order of 1 mm.

An asymptote-matching correlation for hydrodynamic entry length was derived: Lent/D = [(0.54)^1.62 + (0.05 Re)^1.62]^(1/1.62), with entrance length depending linearly on Re at high Re and being constant at low Re.

Radiation was shown to be necessary to correctly capture axial temperature profiles compared to experimental measurements, with effects most significant at the inlet/exit regions and at higher temperatures (e.g., catalytic combustors) rather than lower-temperature EGATS conditions.
Thermocouple-indicated temperatures in a monolith channel can be significantly affected by radiation even when the thermocouple does not block the channel.
Hayes_2021_Multi_scale_modelling_of_mono.nu_correlation: No Nusselt number correlation is given in this excerpt; only a hydrodynamic entry length correlation is reported: Lent/D = [(0.54)^1.62 + (0.05 Re)^1.62]^(1/1.62) (Equation 1), derived via asymptote matching for the single-channel model.
Hayes_2021_Multi_scale_modelling_of_mono.validation_data: Model-predicted axial temperature profiles were compared against experimental axial temperature profile measurements from a monolith reactor.
Hayes_2021_Multi_scale_modelling_of_mono.limitations_stated: Fully 3D models are rare due to high computational cost; 2D axi-symmetric models require assuming a uniform (averaged) washcoat thickness, introducing some error; imposing a flat inlet velocity profile and using a simple upstream reservoir does not correctly capture actual inlet contraction effects on entry length; thermocouple measurements of channel temperature are affected by radiation, causing discrepancies between indicated and actual temperatures; all models contain some form of error and must balance simplicity against fidelity.
Hayes_2021_Multi_scale_modelling_of_mono.relevance: The review's treatment of single-channel monolith modelling, entry-length effects, external heat/mass transfer, and especially radiation's role in axial heat transfer and thermocouple temperature measurement error provides directly relevant modelling context and cautions for interpreting experimental temperature data from an installed SiC honeycomb receiver.

Kribus_2014_The_promise_and_challenge_of.title: The promise and challenge of solar volumetric absorbers
Kribus_2014_The_promise_and_challenge_of.system: A one-dimensional planar slab of ceramic foam (reticulated porous ceramic) volumetric solar absorber for heating air to high temperature.
Kribus_2014_The_promise_and_challenge_of.method: A simplified 1-D model with local thermal non-equilibrium and effective volumetric properties, using the S4 discrete ordinates radiative transfer model (selected via validation against a detailed Monte-Carlo simulation), to parametrically study absorber geometry and material properties.
findings: Predicted absorber efficiency can increase from around 70% to 90% for air heating to 1000 C under incident flux of 800 kW/m2 with combined measures (enhanced convection, reduced solid conductivity, spectral selectivity).
An ideal LTE absorber model predicts efficiency over 95% for 800 kW/m2 incident flux and 1000 C exit air temperature, which is unrealistically optimistic compared to practice.

Reported field/lab absorbers show efficiency around 70%: TSA wire-knit absorber reached air exit temperatures up to 780 C with ~70% efficiency; HITREC ceramic grid absorber achieved ~76% efficiency at 700 C and ~72% at 800 C.
Higher efficiency (80-90%) at exit temperatures >1100 C was reported only under very high incident flux of several thousand suns, impractical for commercial-scale receivers.
Sensitivity study: varying the empirical extinction constant C from 4.1 to 5.5 changed absorber efficiency only slightly, from 0.771 to 0.756 (Table 3).
Kribus_2014_The_promise_and_challenge_of.nu_correlation: The paper references a volumetric Nusselt number definition (Nuv = hv*d^2/kf) and an empirical extinction/absorption correlation (Eq. (4), with empirical constant C, compared against empirical data in Fig. 12), but the specific correlation formula is not given in the extracted text beyond the nomenclature and sensitivity table.
Kribus_2014_The_promise_and_challenge_of.ltne: LTNE is explicitly modeled (not assumed equal, not just measured): solid and fluid temperatures are treated as distinct via effective volumetric properties; the paper contrasts this with the LTE assumption (infinite convective heat transfer coefficient) used in some prior simplified models, and notes LTNE studies show the solid front-surface temperature is higher than or close to deeper temperatures (no real volumetric effect), unlike LTE models which artificially force low front temperature via boundary conditions.
Kribus_2014_The_promise_and_challenge_of.validation_data: The S4 discrete ordinates radiative transfer model was validated against a detailed Monte-Carlo simulation; Eq. (4) (extinction empirical constant) was compared against empirical data (Fig. 12).
Kribus_2014_The_promise_and_challenge_of.limitations_stated: The model does not address additional practical issues such as materials for thermal shock/cycling, the need for a high-pressure window when integrated with a gas turbine cycle, or cycle configuration and economic aspects; the Rosseland/P1 radiative approximations used in some prior works are noted as inappropriate near the absorber front boundary layer, which is not optically thick.
Kribus_2014_The_promise_and_challenge_of.relevance: This paper's LTNE modeling framework, radiative transfer approach, and quantified efficiency/volumetric-effect benchmarks (e.g., front-surface vs. exit temperature behavior, ~70-90% efficiency ranges) provide a theoretical basis and comparison point for interpreting experimental temperature and heat-transfer measurements from an installed SiC honeycomb receiver.

Mendes_2014_detailed_simplified_models_e.title: Detailed and simplified models for evaluation of effective thermal conductivity of open-cell porous foams at high temperatures in presence of thermal radiation
Mendes_2014_detailed_simplified_models_e.journal: International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer
Mendes_2014_detailed_simplified_models_e.system: Open-cell ceramic/metallic porous foam structures, reconstructed from 3D CT-scan images, under coupled conduction-radiation heat transfer at high temperature.
Mendes_2014_detailed_simplified_models_e.method: Detailed 3D finite-volume simulations solving the energy equation coupled with the radiative transfer equation via a blocked-off region approach on voxelized CT-scan geometries, compared against three simplified homogeneous models using pre-computed pure-conduction ETC and CT-derived extinction coefficient.
findings: Superposing separately computed pure-conduction and pure-radiation ETCs does not reproduce the ETC from the combined conduction-radiation model, and the deviation increases with increasing emissivity of internal solid surfaces.
Homogeneous models solving the RTE (coupled or superposed with conduction) give similar predictions, whereas the homogeneous model with the Rosseland approximation slightly over-predicts ETC.
Using the maximum value of extinction coefficient in the converged depth of the sample gives the best agreement with the detailed reference model.

With the maximum extinction coefficient, homogeneous models (except Rosseland) yield relative errors below 10%, but this can rise to about 15% for lower internal surface emissivity due to the role of scattering phase function modelling.
RTE angular discretization used 10x8 control angles (Δθ=18°, Δφ=45°), found sufficient for control-angle-independent solutions.
Mendes_2014_detailed_simplified_models_e.validation_data: Detailed conduction-radiation model results (from the blocked-off region FVM/RTE reference simulation) are used to validate/benchmark the simplified homogeneous models; extinction coefficients are evaluated from 3D CT-scan image processing rather than experiments; the underlying detailed method itself was previously validated against Fluent 6.3 for regular structures in ref. [2].
Mendes_2014_detailed_simplified_models_e.limitations_stated: The investigation is restricted to numerical simulations and comparison of theoretical models only; no experimental validation of the recommended models was performed, and the authors state experimental validation should be carried out as a next step; accuracy of homogeneous models strongly depends on the (non-uniquely defined) extinction coefficient value chosen from CT-scan processing.
Mendes_2014_detailed_simplified_models_e.relevance: Provides a validated numerical framework and simplified homogeneous conduction-radiation models (with ETC and extinction coefficient inputs derivable from CT-scan/structural data) that could be used to interpret or predict effective thermal conductivity behavior of an installed SiC honeycomb receiver operating at high temperature, though it does not itself provide experimental data on installed receivers.

Schlereth_Hinrichsen_2014_Comparison_of_.title: Comparison of a Pseudocontinuous, Heterogeneous 2D Conductive Monolith Reactor Model to a 3D Computational Fluid Dynamics Model
Schlereth_Hinrichsen_2014_Comparison_of_.system: A low-void-fraction, catalytically coated conductive metallic honeycomb (monolith) reactor undergoing an irreversible, exothermic first-order reaction under polytropic operation, with geometry based on Groppi et al.'s o-xylene oxidation honeycomb.
Schlereth_Hinrichsen_2014_Comparison_of_.method: A pseudocontinuous, heterogeneous 2D conductive honeycomb reactor model (using the symmetric effective radial thermal conductivity model, 1D channel-level global heat/mass transfer coefficients) is compared against a detailed 3D CFD model solving coupled laminar flow, species, and heat transport with explicit reaction at the channel wall, both solved in Comsol Multiphysics V4.3.
findings: For reference conditions (DaI = 2.0), maximum solid-phase temperatures between the 2D continuum and 3D CFD models differ by less than 0.5 K.
At higher reaction rates (higher Damköhler numbers), the 3D model predicts systematically higher maximum temperatures and conversions than the continuum model.

Under nonreactive, stagnant-fluid conditions with imposed coaxial heat flux, the symmetric thermal resistance model agrees well with the 3D model, while the series and parallel models under- and overestimate maximum temperature, respectively.
For calculating effective radial properties at this low channel-number monolith, the void fraction of a single, non-deformed channel (0.64) rather than the whole cross-section (0.60) must be used.

If heat transfer from solid to gas phase is neglected entirely, the maximum temperature rises by only about 3 K at the fastest reaction rate studied, showing gas-phase heat removal is a minor contribution to total heat removal.
Mesh refinement study shows differences in maximum temperature of less than 1 K across all mesh sizes tested.
Schlereth_Hinrichsen_2014_Comparison_of_.nu_correlation: The continuum model uses Nusselt and Sherwood number correlations based on the analogy with the Graetz problem for constant wall temperature (as in Groppi and Tronconi's model); no explicit new correlation with numerical range is given in this excerpt.
Schlereth_Hinrichsen_2014_Comparison_of_.ltne: assumed - separate gas-phase and solid-phase enthalpy balances are formulated (local thermal non-equilibrium) coupled via a global heat transfer coefficient (h) in both the 1D channel description of the continuum model and implicitly resolved in the 3D CFD model; the paper notes that heat transfer from solid to gas is only a minor contribution to total heat removal, with maximum temperature rising by only ~3 K if this gas-phase heat transfer term is neglected.
Schlereth_Hinrichsen_2014_Comparison_of_.validation_data: The continuum and 3D models are validated against each other (not against independent experimental data in this excerpt); an analytical plug-flow-reactor (PFR) solution is used to validate isothermal, first-order reaction behavior, and the cumulative residence time distribution is compared to the Aris-Taylor dispersion model for laminar flow in circular tubes.
Schlereth_Hinrichsen_2014_Comparison_of_.limitations_stated: Diffusion limitations inside the washcoat are neglected; gap resistance between honeycomb and tube wall is not addressed; flow is assumed equally distributed over all channels; washcoat resistance and radiation heat transfer are neglected; the first 5 cm of the honeycomb are assumed catalytically inactive, so inlet effects may influence results under harsh conditions; the continuum model assumes a radially fully segregated flow (channel size small compared to tube size), which becomes inaccurate for low channel-number monoliths at high reaction rates where lateral diffusion to hot spots matters; global heat/mass transfer coefficients in the 1D channel model may not adequately capture local transfer coefficients near light-off/harsh conditions.
Schlereth_Hinrichsen_2014_Comparison_of_.relevance: The paper's finding that continuum (homogenized) monolith models using global heat/mass transfer coefficients and effective radial thermal conductivity agree well with detailed 3D simulations only under moderate conditions but deviate at harsh conditions in low channel-number geometries is directly relevant to interpreting and validating heat transfer characterization data from an installed SiC honeycomb receiver, where channel-to-receiver-scale ratios and local thermal non-equilibrium effects may similarly limit the applicability of simplified continuum heat transfer models.

Smirnova_Fend_2011_COMSOL_Solar_Receiver.title: Numeric modelling of a compact high temperature heat exchanger
Smirnova_Fend_2011_COMSOL_Solar_Receiver.system: A compact counter-flow gas/gas heat exchanger made of extruded silicon carbide (SiC) with quadratic channels, alternating between 'direct opened' and 'slotted' channel rows, designed for high-temperature applications (up to 1200°C) such as supporting particle filter regeneration in automobiles.
Smirnova_Fend_2011_COMSOL_Solar_Receiver.method: Two numeric COMSOL-Multiphysics models (a one-variable model at constant velocity and a two-variable model coupling weakly compressible Navier-Stokes with non-isothermal heat transfer) were solved for two-semi-channel and full active-volume geometries, and a 2D model including inlet/outlet regions was compared against prior experimental heat flow data.
findings: The two numeric models (one-variable vs two-variable) differ in predicted temperature by 40–42% for the same sample.
The one-variable model's numeric heat flows between the two heat carriers differ by about 20%, while experimental heat flows between carriers differ by only 3–5%.

Sample 1 (channel cross-section 0.002 m, wall thickness 0.0008 m, porosity 42%) shows about 10% advantage over sample 2 (0.00217 m, 0.00058 m, porosity 53%) in the two-variable model due to smaller convective resistance, but sample 2's experimental advantage reaches 18% versus under 10% numerically.

Reducing channel width by 25% (virtual samples 1.1 and 2.1) increased inside velocity (e.g., sample 1: 4.52→4.81 m/s; sample 2: 4.15→4.4 m/s) and decreased outlet temperature (sample 1: 645→597 K; sample 2: 719→660 K).

Dimensionless velocity/temperature differences between geometries ranged from 0.26–0.45 (velocity) and 0.18–0.33 (temperature), with the largest difference between samples 1 and 2 (both channel width and wall thickness changed) and the smallest for the case with the larger wall thickness.
Smirnova_Fend_2011_COMSOL_Solar_Receiver.validation_data: Experimental heat flow (Q) versus mass flow curves for both heat carriers and both samples, taken from a prior experimental study (ref. [1]), used to compare against the one-variable and two-variable simulation model outputs (Figure 5).
Smirnova_Fend_2011_COMSOL_Solar_Receiver.limitations_stated: The full-geometry (active volume) task could only be solved with the one-variable model because of PC memory capacity limitations; the 3D geometry modeling could not account for the inhomogeneous distribution of velocity and temperature fields, which indirectly explains why the numeric advantage of sample 2 (under 10%) did not match the larger experimental advantage (18%); larger divergence between experimental and numeric results for the second heat carrier was attributed to lower correspondence between experimental and numeric inlet velocity values.
Smirnova_Fend_2011_COMSOL_Solar_Receiver.relevance: This work demonstrates that channel geometry (direct-opened vs slotted) in an extruded SiC honeycomb-type heat exchanger produces strongly inhomogeneous velocity and temperature distributions—especially in slotted channels near inlet/outlet—that reduce effective heat transfer surface and cause significant model-experiment discrepancies, underscoring the need for spatially resolved experimental characterization (not just bulk inlet/outlet measurements) when validating an installed SiC honeycomb receiver's thermal performance.

Wang_Li_et_al_2021_Non_uniform_and_volum.title: Non-uniform and volumetric effect on the hydrodynamic and thermal characteristic in a unit solar absorber
Wang_Li_et_al_2021_Non_uniform_and_volum.system: Four porous silicon carbide (SiC) volumetric solar absorbers with different pore diameters and porosities, tested on a laboratory solar-simulator platform to study non-uniform temperature distribution and hydrodynamic/thermal (volumetric) effects.
Wang_Li_et_al_2021_Non_uniform_and_volum.method: Indoor solar-simulator test rig (solar simulator, porous receiver, air circulation system, water cooling system, data acquisition with thermocouples and infrared thermometers/camera) combined with a three-dimensional local thermal non-equilibrium (LTNE) theoretical model coupling solar radiation transport, thermal conduction, and interphase convection.
findings: A small pore diameter significantly enhances the volumetric heat-transfer coefficient, raising fluid temperature and thermal efficiency.
For absorbers with similar porosity (φ ~ 0.85), decreasing pore diameter dp from 5.83 mm to 2.22 mm increased thermal efficiency η by nearly 3%.
Simulation results show the absorber unit with dp = 2.22 mm and φ = 0.95 exhibits the maximum thermal efficiency of 72.48%.
The solar simulator can emit up to 2.0 kW radiation power with a peak radiative flux density of ~1000 kW/m^2.

Under high local thermal non-equilibrium, non-uniform hydrodynamic behavior is significantly influenced by increased fluid viscosity at the hot spot, especially for small-pore absorbers, raising overheating risk.
Wang_Li_et_al_2021_Non_uniform_and_volum.ltne: Assumed/modeled: the paper explicitly employs an LTNE model (separate solid and fluid energy equations, Section 3.1) to describe convective heat transfer inside the porous SiC absorber; magnitude is discussed qualitatively (high LTNE state causes hot-spot viscosity increase and non-uniform flow) but no single numeric LTNE magnitude (e.g., ΔT between phases) is given in the provided text.
Wang_Li_et_al_2021_Non_uniform_and_volum.validation_data: Surface temperatures measured by two infrared thermometers and an infrared camera, plus thermocouple readings at various platform positions and air outlet temperature, used to characterize non-uniform temperature distribution and (per reference to their prior study [42]) to validate/calibrate the theoretical model.
Wang_Li_et_al_2021_Non_uniform_and_volum.relevance: The paper's findings on how SiC foam pore diameter and porosity govern volumetric heat-transfer coefficient, non-uniform surface temperature, and LTNE-driven hydrodynamic effects provide a directly comparable experimental/modelling basis for interpreting temperature non-uniformity, hot-spot risk, and thermal-efficiency trends when experimentally characterizing an installed SiC honeycomb receiver.

Zaversky_Aldaz_et_al_2018_Numerical_and_.title: Numerical and experimental evaluation and optimization of ceramic foam as solar absorber – Single-layer vs multi-layer configurations
Zaversky_Aldaz_et_al_2018_Numerical_and_.system: Ceramic foam (silicon carbide) volumetric solar absorbers for air-based central receiver/power tower CSP, in single-, double-, and triple-layer configurations.
Zaversky_Aldaz_et_al_2018_Numerical_and_.method: Two independently developed 1-D LTNE models (one using discrete-ordinate radiation transport, the other using Bouguer's-law exponential solar flux attenuation with Rosseland diffusion approximation for thermal radiation) were validated against experimental data from a 4 kW solar simulator and then used in automated parametric optimization studies of absorber thermal efficiency.
findings: A broad plateau-like efficiency maximum occurs for cell densities between 30 and 50 PPI.
The higher the porosity of the foam, the higher the absorber thermal efficiency.

In multi-layer configurations, no significant correlation was observed between efficiency and the properties of the second or third layer; only the first layer's parameters determine thermal performance.
An optimized single-layer configuration is concluded to be the absorber of choice, with a second layer only justified for mechanical stability.
Zaversky_Aldaz_et_al_2018_Numerical_and_.ltne: assumed (local thermal non-equilibrium, LTNE, is incorporated in both 1-D models developed at CENER and Fraunhofer-IKTS, treating solid and fluid as having separate temperature distributions along absorber depth); no specific magnitude given in this excerpt.
Zaversky_Aldaz_et_al_2018_Numerical_and_.validation_data: Both 1-D models were checked for consistency against experimental data obtained at a 4 kW solar simulator.
Zaversky_Aldaz_et_al_2018_Numerical_and_.relevance: The paper's findings on how foam porosity and cell density (PPI) govern thermal efficiency, and its LTNE modeling/validation approach against solar-simulator data, provide a benchmark and methodological reference for experimentally characterizing heat transfer and thermal performance in an installed SiC honeycomb receiver.
